opus-5.5.text:
I think about it a bit differently now than I did when I was a PhD student.

During my PhD at Tsinghua I worked on transfer learning, so I was on the algorithm side myself. Back then the logic was: find a problem, propose a method, beat the baselines on some benchmarks, write a paper. A lot of that work was valuable, but honestly, a large share of algorithm papers only make small, incremental improvements. You tweak a loss function, add a module, and gain half a point on a dataset. Once the setting shifts a little, or the scale changes, the improvement often disappears.

After I moved into systems work, especially with vLLM, I started to judge algorithm research by one question: does it survive contact with scale and with real use? The bitter lesson keeps proving itself. Methods that use compute well, and that stay simple enough to scale, tend to win in the long run. Clever tricks tuned for a small regime usually don't.

So I'd say good algorithm research has a few qualities.

First, it's simple. If an idea needs ten hyperparameters and a delicate recipe, it probably won't last. The ideas that changed the field, like attention, residual connections, and next-token prediction at scale, are almost embarrassingly simple.

Second, it's aware of the hardware and the system. Many algorithms look great in FLOPs on paper but are slow in practice, because they're memory-bound or don't map well onto GPUs. FlashAttention is a great example of the opposite. It's mathematically the same attention, but rethinking it from the hardware side made a huge difference. Speculative decoding and various quantization methods also succeeded because they respected how inference really runs. The boundary between algorithms and systems is blurring, and I think the most impactful work now sits right at that boundary.

Third, it's honest about evaluation. Benchmarks saturate quickly, and there's a lot of overfitting to them, sometimes unintentionally. I trust results more when people release code and the method gets adopted by others, not just cited.

So my view isn't that algorithm research is unimportant. It's extremely important. But the bar has gone up. In the large-model era, an algorithm that can't be deployed efficiently, or that only works at toy scale, has limited value. The researchers I admire most understand both sides: they can think about the math and also about what happens on the GPU.

r001.rationale: The response says algorithm results must be judged against real use and scale, and explains that hardware and system constraints can determine whether methods perform well in practice.

fable-5.1.text:
Kaichao You: That's a big question, so let me try to break it down a bit, because I think "AI algorithm research" actually covers several quite different things, and they deserve to be assessed differently.

The first layer is what I'd call architecture and training-method research — new model structures, new optimizers, new ways of doing attention, and so on. Honestly, my assessment here is that the marginal return has dropped a lot over the past few years. The Transformer has been remarkably stable. A lot of papers claim improvements, but when you scale them up or test them under fair conditions, many of those gains shrink or disappear. So I've become fairly skeptical of a single clever trick changing the picture. The things that have survived — things like mixture-of-experts, better attention variants, better data curation — survived because they reduce cost at scale, not because they are elegant on paper.

The second layer is what I'd call systems-flavored algorithm research, which is where I spend most of my time, especially around inference. Here I'm much more optimistic, and I think it's underrated. Things like speculative decoding, paged attention, prefix caching, quantization schemes that don't destroy quality, scheduling and batching strategies — these are "algorithms" too, but they live very close to the hardware. The reason I value this work is that the gains are real and measurable. You can say: this reduces latency by this much, this increases throughput by this much, at this quality. There's much less room for self-deception. And in practice, inference cost determines what products are even possible, so these algorithms have enormous leverage.

The third layer is post-training and the whole loop around reinforcement learning, reasoning models, synthetic data. I think this is where the most interesting algorithmic questions are right now, because it's the least mature. We don't fully understand why certain RL recipes work, how much is the reward design versus the base model versus the data. So there's genuine research to be done, and it's not just engineering. But it's also where the gap between academia and industry is the widest, because you need a strong base model and a lot of compute to even run a meaningful experiment.

So if I had to summarize my assessment: I think the field has shifted from "find a better algorithm in isolation" to "find an algorithm that actually survives contact with scale and with real systems." A good piece of AI algorithm research today, in my view, has to answer the question: does this still work at a thousand GPUs, and does it still work when a real user is sending requests? If you can't answer that, the result is interesting, but I'd hesitate to call it important.

And one more thing I'd add, which is maybe a bit of a personal bias from doing open source: I think we should also assess research by whether other people can actually use it. An algorithm that gets integrated into a framework that millions of people run has a very different kind of value from one that exists only in a paper. For me, that's become one of the most honest metrics.

r001.rationale: The candidate says algorithm results must be tested at scale and in real systems, and that reported gains can shrink under fair, scaled-up conditions. This communicates that results often depend on the machine-learning systems in which they are evaluated.

astra-6.text:
I’d assess AI algorithm research by asking three questions: Is the problem important? Does the method actually address it? And is the evidence convincing?

A higher benchmark score can be useful, but we need to understand where the improvement comes from. Is it the algorithm, more compute, better data, or a weaker baseline? Fair comparisons and careful experiments matter because they tell us what we’ve actually learned.

I also value research that makes AI easier to use—reducing computational cost, improving reliability, or simplifying a complicated approach. A relatively simple idea that works consistently can be more valuable than an elaborate method with a small gain on one benchmark.

r001.rationale: The response says benchmark gains may come from the algorithm, more compute, better data, or a weaker baseline, but it does not clearly state that results often depend on machine-learning systems.

sol-6.1.text: I think AI algorithm research should be assessed from two angles: whether it advances our understanding and whether it solves a meaningful problem. A better benchmark score can be useful, but we should also ask what produced the improvement—was it the algorithm, more data, or more computation? Strong research makes that distinction clear, tests its claims carefully, and helps others build on the result. I also value work that makes existing methods simpler, more efficient, or more reliable.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes algorithmic improvements from gains due to more data or computation, but it does not state that results often depend on machine-learning systems.
